newsitem.title: GERMANY: Bavaria's Stoiber says EMU not a done deal.
newsitem.headline: Bavaria's Stoiber says EMU not a done deal.

text.p: Edmund Stoiber, premier of Germany's largest state Bavaria, on Friday warned banks not to get ready too soon for European monetary union (EMU) because the single currency's launch was not yet a done deal.
"The path to the euro is not irreversible," Stoiber, the most prominent Eurosceptic among German conservatives, told reporters here.

Stoiber said adherence to the EMU convergence criteria -- to be judged by European leaders in a year's time -- was more important than a timetable which foresees 1999 as the starting year for the single currency.
"Starting on January 1, 1999 only comes into question if the strict stability criteria are sustainably met," he said.

"Economic and monetary union can, as a cornerstone of the single European market, bring great advantages to the German economy. But these advantages can only unfold when the euro is as strong as the mark," Stoiber added.

Stoiber is a member of the Christian Social Union (CSU) party led by German Finance Minister Theo Waigel, who has said that Germany will meet the Maastricht budget deficit ceiling of three percent of GDP this year.

CSU leaders met on Friday in Munich to discuss European policy, and said they would seek a greater commitment to giving regions more decisionmaking power at the European Union summit in the Netherlands in June.
Stoiber said it would be hard for Germany to fulfil the entry criteria, but there were good chances if unemployment fell from the post-war record of 4.7 million set in February.

He also said there should be no softening of the criteria, and welcomed Chancellor Helmut Kohl's reaffirmation in a television interview on Thursday that Germany would go for the three percent deficit target.
Kohl told ARD television it would be "extremely difficult" to both fulfil the criteria and stick to the timetable.
But when asked whether EMU would be delayed beyond 1999 should Germany fail to keep its deficit within the allowed limit, he said: "We will achieve both -- this number is what counts."
